content.note: Figures were verified on September 24, 2026 against official city, county and state publications unless marked otherwise. The engine module docstring defines each base (`state_taxable_income`, `earned_income`, and so on).

The catalog covers taxes a resident owes because of where they live. A plan default or residency period selects one jurisdiction, or custom rates on earned income, state taxable income or state income tax. Custom rates cover localities outside the catalog, for example other Pennsylvania and Ohio municipalities, Ohio school districts and Iowa school district surtaxes.

Not modeled, because they follow work location rather than residence: nonresident wage taxes (Philadelphia, Yonkers, Michigan cities, Ohio work cities), Kentucky occupational license taxes (Louisville, Lexington and others tax only work performed in the jurisdiction), Alabama occupational taxes, Colorado occupational privilege taxes, West Virginia city service fees, the Pennsylvania Local Services Tax, and New York's MCTMT on self-employment earnings. Also not modeled: the NYC Unincorporated Business Tax and its credit, Kansas local intangibles taxes (interest and dividends), and credits for tax paid to a work city.

The residence resolved for a year applies to the whole year, as the state layer does; a move year warns that part-year local tax is not modeled. Taxes on a state-income base inherit the state layer's simplifications, which each entry's limitation text names. Statutory sunsets that are routinely renewed (NYC rates through 2029, the Yonkers surcharge through 2027) are assumed to continue. Voter-approved sunsets are followed (Metro SHS after 2030; East Lansing after 2030).

content.rule: 3.078% / 3.762% / 3.819% / 3.876% on NY taxable income. Thresholds: single and MFS 12,000 / 25,000 / 50,000; MFJ 21,600 / 45,000 / 90,000; HoH 14,400 / 30,000 / 60,000. Not indexed. School tax credits: rate reduction 0.171% to the first threshold and 0.228% above it, only if NYC taxable income is $500,000 or less; fixed $63 ($125 MFJ) if income is $250,000 or less (federal AGI stands in for AGI less IRA distributions). Credits are applied as nonrefundable. The proposed millionaire rate increase was not enacted.
Resident surcharge of 16.75% of net New York State tax.

content.note: The NY state standard deduction was corrected to $8,000 in the same change; see `_sources` in `tax_brackets_2026.json`.

content.rule: Wage and Earnings Tax on gross compensation before employee pre-tax deductions: 3.74% through June 30, 2026 and 3.735% after, so 3.7375% for calendar 2026 wages paid evenly. Net Profits Tax and School Income Tax use the July 1 rate: 3.735% (2026), 3.73% (2027), 3.72% (2028), 3.70% (2029 on), enacted by Bill 250195. School Income Tax base: dividends, investment income streams and non-employer annuities; bank interest, gains held over six months and retirement income are exempt.

content.note: Every county and Baltimore City taxes Maryland taxable income. 2026 rates: 3.20% in Allegany, Baltimore City, Baltimore, Calvert, Caroline, Howard, Montgomery, Prince George's, Queen Anne's, St. Mary's, Somerset and Wicomico; 3.30% in Dorchester and Kent; 3.06% Harford; 3.03% Carroll and Charles; 2.95% Washington; 2.74% Cecil; 2.65% Garrett; 2.40% Talbot; 2.25% Worcester. Anne Arundel is marginal (2.70% / 2.94% / 3.20% with breaks at 50,000 and 400,000; 75,000 and 480,000 joint). Frederick applies one tier rate to all taxable income (2.25% / 2.75% / 2.96% / 3.20%; breaks 25,000, 50,000, 150,000 single and 25,000, 100,000, 250,000 joint). Sources: https://services.marylandcomptroller.gov/taxes/en/maryland-income-tax-rates-and-brackets?id=kb_article_view&sysparm_article=KB0010014, https://www.marylandcomptroller.gov/content/dam/mdcomp/tax/legal-publications/facts/withholding-tax-facts-2026.pdf.

All 92 county rates from Departmental Notice #1, effective January 1, 2026 (https://www.in.gov/dor/files/dn01.pdf), applied to Indiana taxable income. The county of residence on January 1 governs. Re-check after October 1, 2026: a county adopting a new rate then pays three quarters of the old rate and one quarter of the new one for 2026. SEA 1 (2025) lets cities levy their own rates from 2028.

All 24 taxing cities (https://www.michigan.gov/taxes/citytax/what-cities-impose-an-income-tax). Resident rates: Detroit 2.4%, Highland Park 2.0%, Grand Rapids and Saginaw 1.5%, the others 1.0%. Exemption per person: $600, except Ionia $700; Battle Creek, Saginaw, Benton Harbor and Springfield $750; Hudson and Portland $1,000; Grayling $3,000. Taxpayer and spouse exemptions plus one more for each person 65 or older. The base follows the Detroit resident return (Form 5118): federal AGI less taxable Social Security, pensions, annuities and retirement-plan distributions. Detroit: https://www.michigan.gov/taxes/-/media/Project/Websites/taxes/Forms/City-IIT/TY2026/5123_2026.pdf. Benton Harbor and Springfield figures come from Grand Rapids' table of other cities, because both city sites blocked retrieval.

content.rule: 1% of Oregon taxable income above $128,000 (single, MFS) or $205,000 (MFJ, HoH, QSS) in 2026; thresholds indexed (Ordinance 25-1531); tax ends after 2030.
1.5% above $125,000 / $200,000 plus 1.5% above $250,000 / $400,000; not indexed. The 0.8-point increase to the first tier (2.3%) is scheduled for 2028 after the August 27, 2026 delay.
From 2026: $50 per return ($100 MFJ) when Oregon taxable income exceeds $20,000 ($40,000 MFJ, HoH, QSS); indexed from 2027.

content.note: The Portland entry combines all three; other entries cover Multnomah County inside or outside Metro and the Metro district in Clackamas or Washington County.

content.rule: Resident rate on Medicare wages plus net profits (ORC 718): Columbus, Cleveland, Toledo, Akron, Dayton, Canton, Parma, Lorain 2.5%; Youngstown 2.75%; Cincinnati 1.8%. Parma and Lorain credit tax paid to a work city only up to 2.0%.
1% earnings tax on W-2 box 1 wages plus net profits; deferred-compensation and cafeteria contributions are excluded (RSMo 92.113). Renewed April 7, 2026.
1.25% on residents' gross earned income and on net profits (22 Del. C. §§901–902). Whether 401(k) deferrals are included is not published; gross wages are used.
